A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same joint-likelihood OOD detection study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–D are sufficiently complete and readable for reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on toy regression, PDE prediction, humidity forecasting, image classification, and brain tumor segmentation, including numerical comparisons and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds AUROC measurements, computational-cost experiments, and comparisons with Bayesian uncertainty methods.

M1.justification: The joint-likelihood algorithm, Algorithm 1, and classification/segmentation adaptations remain unchanged. However, B.1.7 introduces a newly trained JLBC* variant containing dropout with p=0.1 for the Bayesian comparison, constituting a limited model adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same toy functions, wave and Navier–Stokes distributions, MERRA-2 regions, CIFAR-10/MNIST/SVHN scenarios, and BraTS populations, modalities, and slice orientations. The added experiments use existing wave-equation coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct wave-equation comparisons against MC-Dropout and Rate-In in B.1.7, Table 4, and Figure 17. This substantially broadens the evaluated alternatives to Bayesian uncertainty methods. Existing diffusion, OODC, input-only, and persistence comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds threshold-independent ROC/AUROC evaluation across the scientific comparisons and new wave experiments varying stochastic-estimator budgets. The Bayesian comparison includes dropout-trained JLBC* and specifies mean-plus/minus-1.5-standard-deviation thresholds. Existing dataset splits and training-setting tables are retained; the single RK38 integration step is newly disclosed rather than established as a changed original setting.

E4.justification: New B.1.6 tests how divergence-estimator tensor sizes of 32, 8, and 2 affect computation time and detection performance; B.1.7 also varies Bayesian sampling budgets. Earlier architectural, calibration, temporal, noise-injection, and percentile-band analyses remain. The training-distribution error fits highlighted in the main text already appeared in v1.

E5.justification: The ten-model repetitions and median reporting in A.2, and percentile deviation bands in B.4, are retained. v2 adds no benchmark confidence intervals, repeated-training-run reporting, or significance tests. AUROC is a discrimination metric, despite the new text associating it with statistical significance.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in the retained comparison and ablation tables are unchanged. v2 adds AUROC across Table 1, including NS-MIX scores of 0.992 for JLBC and 0.918 for JDPath, plus runtime/sensitivity results in Table 3 and Bayesian comparisons in Table 4. JLBC* reaches AUROC 0.955 under its new configuration; this is newly reported evidence, not an unchanged-setting improvement over v1.

T1.justification: v1's approximate equality based on uniformly distributed training error is replaced by a high-probability upper-bound derivation in A.1 and revised Equation 3.2. v2 introduces power-loss assumptions, exceptional sets, a probability inequality, and a log-Lipschitz argument substituting predicted outputs. The derivation also invokes the density restriction p(x,y)≤1.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: task-aware joint-likelihood certification, zero-shot OOD detection, optional posterior error estimation, and applicability across scientific regression, classification, and segmentation.

C2.justification: A.1 newly explains the bound's assumptions, their possible failure, and why low likelihood need not imply high error. v2 also interprets the added experiments as demonstrating practical speed and Bayesian-method superiority. Its claim of faster evaluation than both Bayesian baselines overstates Table 4, where MC-Dropout is faster at matched tensor counts.

D1.justification: B.1.6 newly specifies one RK38 integration step with four internal stages and RTX 4090 hardware; B.1.7 documents dropout and sampling budgets. Conversely, D.1 drops v1's explicit statement that OODC trains on input/prediction pairs. The architecture specifications and code-access information otherwise remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work adds Gal and Ghahramani, Zeevi et al., and Chan et al. to discuss Bayesian/dropout and hybrid uncertainty estimation. v2 also explicitly attributes JSFNS to this work. Duplicate references are consolidated without removing distinct cited works; the central scientific-regression positioning remains.

P1.justification: v2 makes sentence-level revisions throughout the appendices, converts numbered Results subsections into run-in headings, promotes CIFAR-10 and MNIST appendix headings, and expands the main-text discussion of existing training-distribution analyses. It also adds an LLM-writing disclosure. The overall narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, Table 1 gains AUROC rows, and new Tables 3–4 and Figure 17 display computational and Bayesian comparisons. New Figure 3 combines an existing NS-PwC error-fit panel with new ROC curves. Other displays are largely retained, with localized relocation, resizing, and caption edits.

improvement.justification: The added threshold-independent comparisons, Bayesian baselines, and measured computation–accuracy tradeoffs improve empirical support and practical reproducibility beyond v1. The gains are qualified by A.1's unestablished density bound p(x,y)≤1 and overstated statistical-significance and speed language. For example, Table 4 reports 0.002 seconds for MC-Dropout versus 0.020 seconds for JLBC* at tensor size 2, contradicting the broad speed claim.
